paragraphs: The oldest of all societies, and the only natural one, is the family. Even so, children remain attached to their father only as long as they need him to survive. As soon as that need ends, the natural bond dissolves. The children, released from the obedience they owed the father, and the father, released from the care he owed his children, all return equally to independence. If they stay united, they no longer do so naturally but voluntarily; and the family itself is then held together only by convention.

This common liberty results from the nature of man. His first law is to look after his own preservation, and his first cares are those he owes to himself. As soon as he reaches the age of reason, he is the only judge of the right means of preserving himself, and so becomes his own master.

The family, then, may be called the first model of political societies: the ruler corresponds to the father and the people to the children; and all, being born free and equal, give away their liberty only for their own advantage. The whole difference is that in the family the father’s love for his children repays him for the care he takes of them, while in the State the pleasure of commanding takes the place of the love that the chief cannot have for the peoples under him.

Grotius denies that all human power is established for the benefit of the governed, and he cites slavery as an example. His usual method of reasoning is always to establish right by fact.[1] A more logical method would be possible, but none could be more favorable to tyrants.

According to Grotius, then, it is doubtful whether the human race belongs to a hundred men, or those hundred men belong to the human race; and throughout his book he seems to lean toward the first alternative, which is also the view of Hobbes. On this view, the human species is divided into so many herds of cattle, each with its ruler, who guards them in order to devour them.

Just as a shepherd is of a nature superior to that of his flock, the shepherds of men, that is, their rulers, are of a nature superior to that of the peoples under them. This, Philo tells us, was the reasoning of the Emperor Caligula, who concluded equally well either that kings were gods or that men were beasts.

Caligula’s reasoning agrees with that of Hobbes and Grotius. Aristotle, before any of them, had said that men are by no means equal by nature, but that some are born for slavery and others for mastery.

Aristotle was right, but he mistook the effect for the cause. Nothing is more certain than that every man born in slavery is born for slavery. Slaves lose everything in their chains, even the desire to escape them: they love their servitude, as the companions of Ulysses loved their brutish condition.[2] So if there are slaves by nature, it is because there were slaves against nature. Force made the first slaves, and their cowardice kept them slaves.

I have said nothing of King Adam, or Emperor Noah, father of the three great monarchs who divided up the universe, like the children of Saturn, whom some scholars have recognized in them. I hope to be thanked for my restraint; for, as a direct descendant of one of these princes, perhaps of the eldest branch, how do I know that a check of the titles might not prove me the legitimate king of the human race? In any case, there is no doubt that Adam was sovereign of the world, as Robinson Crusoe was of his island, as long as he was its only inhabitant; and this empire had the advantage that the monarch, safe on his throne, had no rebellions, wars or conspirators to fear.
